newsitem.title: USA: GM says Hughes announcement may not be far off.
newsitem.headline: GM says Hughes announcement may not be far off.

text.p: General Motors Corp., continuing to keep investors in suspense on the expected sale of its Hughes Electronics Corp. defense operations, said Wednesday that a major announcement for Hughes might not be far off.
"If this went months, I'd be in big trouble," Hughes Chairman C. Michael Armstrong told reporters here.
Armstrong, who spoke to the Economic Club of Detroit, declined to comment directly on the possible transaction, which has captivated the defense industry for weeks.
Asked if GM would announce a deal soon, GM Chairman Jack Smith, who also attended Wednesday's luncheon said, "Not today."
Smith said Sunday that GM was trying to get "top dollar" in bidding for the Hughes missile, radar and defense electronics assets.

The auto giant has received acquisition bids for the Hughes defense operations in the $10 billion range from both Raytheon Co. and Northrop Grumman Corp., according to sources familiar with the situation.

Defense industry analysts also said Wednesday that Raytheon has been meeting with bond ratings agencies this week in an effort to head off a possible downgrade of its debt ratings if it was successful in buying the Hughes assets.
Raytheon earlier this week had reportedly gained an edge in the bidding contest.
In his presentation to the Economic Club, Armstrong said Hughes would participate in the defense industry's continuing consolidation, but would not specify how.

He declined to discuss how GM might change the future structure of Hughes assets such as its automotive electronics business and its telecommunications business. But he said Hughes' Delco Electronics divsion will continue to work more closely with GM's Delphi Automotive Systems components arm.

Automotive analysts have said GM was likely to fold Delco back into Delphi after a Hughes defense deal. GM also does not intend to sell its lucrative telecommunications and space business, which includes the fast-growing DirecTV satellite broadcast service.

Spokesmen for Raytheon and ratings agency Moody's Investor Service declined to comment Wednesday on inquiries about meetings. Standard & Poors Corp. said it did not hold any meetings with Raytheon Wednesday.

"Raytheon is meeting with the bond rating people. There's some hint that they're considering taking them to junk bond status and Raytheon doesn't want that," said one analyst. "But it looks like the basic deal has been handed out to them so they can really review it."
